summary.text: Gambler's ruin is the fact that a gambler playing a game that is not in their favor will eventually go bankrupt, no matter what betting system they use.
Even in a fair game, a gambler with limited money who keeps playing against an opponent with unlimited money will eventually go broke.
The idea comes from a theorem by Christiaan Huygens and led to important advances in the mathematical theory of probability.

facts.label: Core claim
facts.value: A non-positive expected value game ends in bankruptcy, whatever the betting system

paragraphs.heading: The idea
paragraphs.text: Gambler's ruin is the fact that someone who plays a game with non-positive expected value will go bankrupt in the end, whatever betting system they use. Another version covers a fair game, where each bet has expected value of zero for both sides. A persistent gambler with limited money, facing an opponent with unlimited money, will still go broke for certain. This situation can be modelled as a random walk on the real number line.

paragraphs.heading: Huygens and the oldest version
paragraphs.text: In the random walk picture, the gambler is all but certain to come back to the starting point, which means going broke. That outcome follows as a corollary from a general theorem of Christiaan Huygens, which also goes by the name gambler's ruin. Given each player's starting stake and a fixed chance of winning each bet, it shows how to work out each player's chance of winning a series that runs until one side loses everything. It is the oldest mathematical idea to carry the name, though not the first idea the name was given to. Huygens's result went on to drive major progress in how mathematicians understand probability.

paragraphs.heading: A game with three dice
paragraphs.text: The classic problem pits two players against each other with three dice. The first scores whenever 11 is rolled, the second whenever 14 is rolled. In one form, each starts with 12 points, and a successful roll adds a point to the roller and takes one from the opponent. Whoever reaches zero first loses. This is the standard picture: two players start with fixed stakes and pass points back and forth until one is ruined, although the name gambler's ruin came much later.

paragraphs.heading: Raising the stakes
paragraphs.text: The idea was first stated about a particular habit. Let d be the gambler's money at any moment and N any positive integer, and suppose they raise their stake to d/N after a win but never lower it after a loss. Then N losses in a row are enough to bankrupt them. If the chance of winning each bet is below 1, they are virtually certain to suffer such a streak eventually, however big N is. This holds even when each bet has positive expected value.

paragraphs.heading: Doubling or going broke
paragraphs.text: In a fair game with a 1/2 chance of winning each bet, the gambler will sooner or later either go broke or double their wealth. By symmetry, each outcome has a 1/2 chance of coming first. If they double up and keep playing, they again face a 1/2 chance of ruin before the next doubling. After two such rounds, the chance they are still solvent is (1/2) ² = 1/4. A player in a game with negative expected value can do no better than this, so they go broke too.

paragraphs.heading: Pennies on the table
paragraphs.text: Picture two players flipping a coin, each with a 50% chance of winning each flip. The loser of each flip hands one penny to the winner, and play ends when one player holds every penny. With no other limit on the number of flips, the game ends this way with probability 1. Even though the odds are equal, the player who starts with fewer pennies is more likely to be ruined.

paragraphs.heading: More than two players
paragraphs.text: The two-player game is a special case of the N-Player Ruin problem. There, N ≥ 2 players start with capital x₁, x₂, …, x_N dollars. They play a sequence of independent games, winning and losing money to each other under fixed rules, and the sequence stops once at least one player is ruined.
